query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy, degradation during high‐temperature exposure is primarily controlled by the selective oxidation of the reactive elements (especially Al and Ti) that migrate to the surface and form a coherent oxide scale. Under oxidizing conditions this scale is protective, preserving the integrity of the fcc matrix and mechanical performance; in reducing environments, the inhibition or absence of this scale results in more rapid degradation via internal oxidation or destabilization.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix and nominal composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 that has demonstrated high strength and fatigue resistance.
generation.intervention: Elevated-temperature exposure (around 750 °C) in environments controlled to be either oxidizing (e.g., air or elevated O2 partial pressure) or reducing (e.g., H2-containing atmospheres).
generation.conditions: Exposure to the specified gas atmospheres at ~750 °C for durations (e.g., 10 h, 25 h, and 50 h) to probe temporal evolution, while maintaining identical heating and cooling protocols across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or lack) of a continuous, coherent oxide scale—rich in Al- and Ti-oxides—mediates the protective effect, ensuring the fcc matrix remains largely unaltered under oxidizing conditions.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, Al and Ti preferentially oxidize and diffuse toward the surface. In oxidizing atmospheres, this leads to the rapid establishment of a protective oxide layer that limits further oxygen ingress and bulk degradation. In reducing environments, the absence or transient nature of this scale allows for more extensive internal oxidation or phase destabilization, which could degrade mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, a continuous and protective oxide scale will be observed along with slower degradation (lower oxidation penetration and retained mechanical integrity). In reducing conditions, incomplete or poorly adherent surface oxides will lead to increased internal degradation and a more rapid loss of mechanical performance relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The untreated alloy exhibits a well-preserved fcc matrix and high strength/fatigue performance with minimal degradation when exposed briefly at high temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for exposures at around 750 °C in atmospheres ranging from strongly oxidizing (e.g., air with high O2 partial pressure) to strongly reducing (e.g., a reducing H2-containing gas). Deviations outside this temperature range or gas compositions may invoke other degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nature, thickness, and composition of the oxide layer (e.g., the balance between alumina and titania phases) as well as the kinetics of diffusion and scale formation may vary with slight compositional or processing differences. The magnitude of mechanical property retention versus degradation under reducing conditions is also not fully predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of alloy samples from the same additively manufactured batch. Expose each set to a fixed temperature (e.g., 750 °C) for varied durations (10, 25, and 50 hours) under two controlled gas environments: a strongly oxidizing condition (pure O2 or air) and a strongly reducing condition (e.g., 5% H2 in N2). After exposure, use scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize the surface and cross-sectional oxide scale morphology, phase composition, and degradation depth. In parallel, perform mechanical tests (e.g., microhardness or fatigue testing) to assess the retention of mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxide scale continuity and thickness (via SEM/TEM)
Phase identification of oxides (via XRD or EDS in TEM)
Measured oxidation/degradation depth into the alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples exposed in oxidizing conditions do not show a significantly more continuous or protective oxide scale compared to those in reducing conditions – or if the degradation (both in depth and in loss of mechanical properties) is comparable between the two gas exposures – then the hypothesis that selective oxidation of Al and Ti leading to a protective scale governs degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Microstructure-Property Correlation and Its Evolution during Aging in an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C.
